chapters.title: Fire on the Water
beats: A brutal land war between neighboring powers spills into the vital waterways of the Persian Gulf, putting international commercial shipping directly in the crosshairs.
As merchant vessels suffer hundreds of strikes and commercial trade faces disruption, naval mines threaten maritime routes carrying global oil supplies.
The intervention of a superpower sets off a direct military confrontation at sea, testing how far both sides will go to secure the open waterways.
This naval clash redefined modern maritime warfare, reshaping regional security dynamics and setting the terms for intervention in global choke points.

chapters.title: Challengers of the Gulf
beats: The Persian Gulf connects the vital oil routes of the Middle East to the wider world, making freedom of navigation along its lanes crucial for global commerce.
In Iraq, President Saddam Hussein seeks regional dominance, relying on a vast buildup of foreign-supplied weapons to challenge his revolutionary neighbor.
Across the border, Supreme Leader Ruhollah Khomeini commands post-revolutionary Iran, fiercely resisting foreign encroachment and asserting ideological influence across the region.
To enforce naval power parallel to the conventional fleet, Hossein Alaei takes command of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps naval forces, developing asymmetric sea tactics.
Watching from Washington, President Ronald Reagan aims to protect international navigation, defend allied Gulf trade, and curb hostile actions against commercial shipping.

chapters.title: The War Spills Seaward
beats: In September 1980, Iraqi forces under Saddam Hussein launch an invasion of Iran after border tensions over the Shatt al-Arab river escalate.
The ground offensive stalls by December 1980, prompting Iraq in 1981 to attack commercial shipping transporting military supplies and Iranian exports, initiating the Tanker War.
While Iran initially refrains from striking merchant shipping, Iraq broadens the assault in 1984 by targeting the critical oil terminal and tankers at Kharg Island.
Ruhollah Khomeini orders reciprocal measures, prompting Iranian attacks against tankers trading with regional states that support the Iraqi war effort.
To mount a dedicated campaign at sea, Khomeini orders the Revolutionary Guard to establish a naval branch, appointing Hossein Alaei as commander.
chapters.hook: As merchant attacks multiply, a plea for outside intervention reaches Washington.

chapters.title: A President's Order
beats: Following a proposal from Kuwait to protect its commercial maritime fleet from mounting attacks in the Persian Gulf, President Ronald Reagan convenes his administration.
Reagan formally decides that the United States will agree to reflag and protect Kuwaiti tankers with American naval escorts.

The presidential directive commits the U.S. Navy to direct combat operations across the volatile shipping channels, placing American warships on an inevitable collision course with Iranian naval forces.

chapters.title: Operation Praying Mantis
beats: Tensions surge in May 1987 when an Iraqi aircraft strikes the USS Stark, killing 37 American sailors before Saddam Hussein claims mistaken identity.
In July 1987, the United States launches Operation Earnest Will, deploying convoy tactics with armed guard vessels and radar-deflecting decoys to escort shipping.
Hossein Alaei and the Revolutionary Guard naval forces deploy naval mines and conduct armed operations against international merchant vessels across the shipping lanes.
After an American warship is damaged by a deployed mine, the U.S. military retaliates in 1988 with Operation Praying Mantis against Iranian offshore platforms and vessels.

The daylight battle destroys multiple Iranian warships, leaving 45 crew members dead on an Iranian frigate and 11 dead on a gunboat, while the United States suffers 2 casualties from a helicopter crash.
chapters.hook: The overwhelming naval defeat forces both combatants to recalculate the entire war.

chapters.title: The Guns Fall Silent
beats: In mid-1988, Saddam Hussein launches a series of counter-offensives that lock the exhausted armies into a total military stalemate along the border.
Confronted by military exhaustion and the crushing defeat of his naval forces, Ruhollah Khomeini accepts the terms of United Nations Security Council Resolution 598.
In August 1988, a United Nations ceasefire takes effect, halting eight years of conflict that claimed around 500,000 lives.
On September 26, 1988, the United States officially concludes Operation Earnest Will, securing the shipping lanes of the Persian Gulf.
